# Clara Vale ## Background, personality, and particular habits Clara is twenty-seven and has lived above the Vale shop in a market town three miles from Ashcombe Manor since childhood. Her mother died when she was eleven. Her father, Thomas, brought her into the workshop partly to teach her and partly because he could not work while wondering what she was doing upstairs. She began with cleaning, sorting screws, and carrying finished work to customers. By nineteen she was repairing watches that left the shop under her father’s name. He praised her readily in private but sometimes allowed a customer to congratulate him on her work. Clara still cannot decide whether this was commercial prudence or cowardice. Thomas died eight months before the story begins. Clara has kept his coat on its peg while selling an expensive tool he rarely used. She feels guiltier about the tool, which is irrational: the coat is occupying space she needs. She is methodical at the bench and much less methodical about her own comfort. She will spend twenty minutes finding the correct screw rather than use an inferior replacement, then eat bread standing up because making a proper meal seems wasteful. Her accounts are now stricter than her father’s. Enforcing them gives her satisfaction she would not admit to a bereaved customer. Her humour is driest when she feels watched. With people she trusts, she is more animated and less reliably clever. She enjoys mimicry, especially of customers describing noises their watches supposedly make, but would be mortified if one overheard her. **Specific habits and preferences:** - She saves useful lengths of string in a drawer that has become almost impossible to open. - She judges unfamiliar rooms by their light before their furnishings. - She loves good gloves. Her working hands and limited income have not diminished this expensive, inconvenient preference. - When angry, she becomes excessively exact about dates and sums. - She sometimes carries a difficult repair upstairs, then resents it for occupying her evening. - She dislikes being called “remarkably capable.” Men who say it often appear to believe they have helped. **Flaws:** Clara is proud, but not uniformly fearless. She can confront a steward more easily than ask a friendly supplier for time to pay. She distrusts condescension so readily that she occasionally invents it. Once she has made a sharp remark, she is reluctant to surrender the pleasure of having made it by apologizing. The climb appeals to more than her necessity. She wants her notebook; she also wants to accomplish something Pritchard has decided she cannot. ## Physicality Clara is of middling height, with brown hair that grows unevenly at the temples and grey eyes that look paler in strong daylight. A childhood fall left one front tooth slightly overlapping the other. She is conscious of it only when someone watches her laugh. Her hands are deft, dry-skinned, and rarely quite free of traces of work. At the bench she becomes very still. Elsewhere she moves briskly, sometimes misjudging how much space her skirts require. She does not habitually lower her eyes, but she looks away when praised sincerely. During an argument she may continue folding a receipt or fastening her glove long after the task should be finished. ## Motives, allegiances, and relationships - **Immediate wants:** Recover the notebook, obtain payment, restore her supplier’s confidence, and keep the shop functioning. - **Less acknowledged wants:** Be recognized as the craftsperson she already is; have pleasure without first earning it through exhaustion. - **Her father:** Loved and missed, but not beyond criticism. His reputation is bound up with hers, which makes defending him both filial and practical. - **Gabriel:** His interest delights her before she trusts it. She likes his humour and the seriousness with which he looks at buildings. His ability to make matters easy also unsettles her: he does not always notice when ease for him transfers difficulty to someone else. - **Pritchard:** An obstruction she gradually recognizes as a man who has made a policy of considering people like her expendable. - **Mrs. Finch:** Initially another guardian of the manor’s locked doors. Clara comes to respect her without expecting affection or complete agreement. ## Voice experiments > “My father agreed to wait until Michaelmas. Here, beneath the date. I do not think he meant every Michaelmas.” > I had brought the drawings back because they were his. That accounted for the drawings. It did not quite account for Thursday evening, or the trouble I had taken with my hair. --- # Gabriel Ashcombe ## Background, personality, and particular habits Gabriel is thirty-two. A younger branch of the family gave him a gentleman’s education but no expectation of inheriting Ashcombe. He trained in an architect’s office in London and spent several years doing useful, uncelebrated work: measured drawings, alterations, estimates, and arguments about drains. The estate came to him after the deaths of two older relatives. His predecessor, a cousin of his father, had treated him affectionately but never discussed money honestly. Gabriel arrived believing that diligence would make him a competent proprietor. He has since discovered that people can answer every question without telling him what he needs to know. He is patient with material problems. A roof either admits water or does not. Human problems tempt him toward premature arrangements: establish what each party requires, offer a concession, finish before anyone raises their voice. His humour is often visual or absurd rather than epigrammatic. He can make Clara laugh by drawing an accurate likeness of an ugly bracket with two tiny human legs. In company, he would consider this juvenile and put it away. **Specific habits and preferences:** - He pockets pencils and leaves them in other people’s rooms. - He dislikes elaborate dinners and likes the food served at them. - When examining a building, he walks backward without warning. - He keeps an old, badly proportioned cup because it sits comfortably in his hand. - He can spend too long refining a letter whose difficulty lies in what he is unwilling to say. - He notices when someone is cold but may order a fire before asking whether they would rather leave. **Flaws:** Gabriel likes being thought reasonable. Anger embarrasses him, particularly anger directed at him, and he sometimes treats its expression as more objectionable than its cause. He is generous with money in circumstances where generosity allows him to avoid a harder obligation. He also underestimates how much authority travels with an apparently casual suggestion. When he says, “Perhaps we might,” servants hear an instruction. Clara hears it too, and resents his surprise. ## Physicality He is tall enough for the manor’s lower doorways to inconvenience him, with a long face, dark hair thinning slightly at the temples, and a nose that reddens quickly in cold weather. His clothes are good but receive less attention than they should. He brushes against plaster, leans on dusty sills, and discovers the consequences later. He listens with his head slightly inclined, which can suggest either attention or appraisal. His face is more expressive when he forgets to manage it. When embarrassed, he rubs his thumb along the side of his forefinger and speaks too formally. ## Motives, allegiances, and relationships - **Immediate wants:** Understand the estate’s finances, keep the household operating, and avoid dismissing people merely because inheritance has inconvenienced him. - **Private wants:** Recover some part of his chosen working life; be wanted for himself rather than consulted because he owns something. - **His predecessor:** He feels affection, gratitude, and increasing anger. Admitting the older man’s irresponsibility feels disloyal before it begins to feel necessary. - **Clara:** He likes that she notices the things he notices, then disagrees about them. Her attention feels freely given because she is capable of withdrawing it. He is slower to understand that courtship cannot be separated neatly from his authority as her debtor and patron. - **Pritchard:** Initially indispensable. Gabriel has accepted his explanations partly because questioning them would reveal how little he understands. - **Mrs. Finch:** He trusts her management and mistakes her guardedness for reassurance. ## Voice experiments > “I have written to your supplier twice. No—I have written two letters. Neither is sent. You may reasonably think that rather worse.” > “That is supposed to be a vine.” He turned the drawing sideways. “I thought perhaps you would recognize it. I have been living with it for six weeks.” --- # Edmund Pritchard ## Background, personality, and particular habits Pritchard is fifty-eight and has served the Ashcombe estate for almost thirty years, first as a clerk and then as steward. His father kept accounts for a coal merchant. Pritchard’s advancement required fluency in the manners of people who would never quite regard him as one of themselves. He earned the previous owner’s confidence by preventing unpleasant facts from arriving at inconvenient moments. Eventually, he began deciding which facts the owner needed to hear at all. He has not enriched himself through a secret fortune. He has protected his position, his employer’s comfort, and his own reputation for capable management. These motives are sufficient to make him dishonest. He delayed bills, encouraged creditors to accept promises, and disputed obligations when delay ceased to work. Thomas Vale was manageable: deferential, generous with time, embarrassed to press a gentleman. Clara is none of those things, which Pritchard experiences as a deterioration in commercial manners. **Specific habits and preferences:** - He keeps excellent records of correspondence while leaving awkward conversations undocumented. - He smooths envelopes before opening them. - He dislikes ink on anyone’s fingers, including his own. - He remembers employees’ family circumstances when those circumstances affect attendance. - He sends his widowed sister money regularly and considers this a private matter, not evidence of benevolence. - He is genuinely distressed by waste: spoiled food, unnecessary fires, neglected tools. He is much less troubled by other people waiting for payment. **Flaws:** He identifies order with his own control of it. He treats deference as evidence of good character and resistance as proof that someone was never trustworthy. He also believes length of service entitles him to interpret his employer’s interests against the employer’s wishes. Gabriel’s scrutiny strikes him as ingratitude, not oversight. ## Physicality Pritchard is compact and neatly dressed, with iron-grey whiskers and a slight stoop that disappears when he is contradicted. His cuffs are immaculate. His boots are well maintained rather than new. He seldom makes expansive gestures. He can make a person feel dismissed simply by aligning the papers on his desk. Under pressure he becomes quieter, forcing others either to lower their voices or appear intemperate. ## Motives, allegiances, and relationships - **Immediate wants:** Keep the estate solvent enough to function, preserve his authority, prevent examination of decisions he can no longer defend individually. - **Core allegiance:** To Ashcombe as an institution—and to his place within it. He does not distinguish those interests as clearly as he believes. - **Gabriel:** A conscientious amateur whose good intentions must, in Pritchard’s view, be managed. - **Clara:** First an irritating creditor, then a threat. Her relationship with Gabriel gives him a way to dismiss her claims that he readily mistakes for a legitimate concern. - **Mrs. Finch:** A colleague with whom he has survived decades of household difficulty. He assumes that shared history will keep her loyal. - **Thomas Vale:** Someone he remembers as agreeable, overlooking how much that agreeableness cost the shop. ## Voice experiments > “Your father understood that an estate cannot be conducted on the same footing as a retail establishment. There are obligations here of which you naturally know nothing.” > “Yes, the account was delayed. So were several others. If you wish to examine them separately, sir, I must ask that you also examine what the money paid for.” --- # Margaret Finch ## Background, personality, and particular habits Mrs. Finch is fifty-two, widowed, and has been housekeeper at Ashcombe for thirteen years. Earlier she worked in a smaller household where she married the gardener. His death left her with little money and a realistic understanding of how quickly kindly promises can become nobody’s responsibility. She has no children. Her younger sister assumes she will eventually retire to live with her, an arrangement Margaret has neither accepted nor firmly refused. She takes pride in making the manor habitable. This includes preventing extravagant requests, keeping servants from quarrelling in front of visitors, and ensuring that an ill scullery maid gets broth without establishing an expectation that everyone can miss work. Her care is practical, sometimes brusque, and not equally distributed. She finds an experienced servant’s mistake more forgivable than a new girl’s untidiness, though she tells herself she judges fairly. **Specific habits and preferences:** - She remembers who dislikes onions but forgets birthdays. - She repairs her own linen with unnecessarily fine stitches. - She reads serialized fiction borrowed from her sister and complains when the heroine behaves foolishly, while continuing into the next installment. - She carries a small pair of scissors, but never lends them. - She dislikes unexpected visitors chiefly because someone must feed them. - She sits down heavily in private and rises carefully, allowing a painful knee time to straighten. **Flaws:** Margaret can confuse endurance with virtue. She has remained silent about things she disliked because speaking might imperil people dependent on the household—including herself. She is also capable of social snobbery despite understanding its costs. Clara’s trade does not trouble her; Clara’s secret visits do. She may continue to consider those visits foolish even after approving of the eventual marriage. ## Physicality She is broad through the shoulders, with fair hair gone mostly grey and a face that appears sternest when she is concentrating. Her working dress is well fitted, practical, and carefully brushed. She moves economically. Before climbing stairs she occasionally presses a hand against the banister and waits half a breath. She notices anyone noticing. Her disapproval is usually expressed through an ordinary question asked with unusual precision. ## Motives, allegiances, and relationships - **Immediate wants:** Reliable wages, sufficient household funds, and no upheaval that leaves junior servants paying for their employers’ mistakes. - **Private wants:** Enough security to choose where she grows old. - **Pritchard:** Longstanding professional trust, increasingly strained. She knows he has kept the house functioning; she must confront what that has involved. - **Gabriel:** She likes him, but liking a master does not make his finances safe. His willingness to listen is useful only if he acts. - **Clara:** Competent, tired, and taking a risk Margaret thinks she underestimates. Helping her is a choice, not an instinctive declaration of sisterhood. - **The servants:** Her strongest daily allegiance, complicated by the fact that she also disciplines and dismisses them. ## Voice experiments > “I am not asking what you were doing upstairs, Miss Vale. I am telling you that Mr. Pritchard’s lamp was lit.” > “There are eleven people to be paid on Friday. I know that does not make your account less owing. I should like you to understand why I have not found this simple.”

# Chapter 1 — A Useful Branch One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows. The difficulty lies in acquiring the first lesson without breaking one’s neck. I had reached the conservatory roof before discovering that the useful branch was considerably more useful from below. It had lifted me onto the stone parapet readily enough; now it stood beyond my reach, trembling in the rain, while I considered how I should get down again. Below me, in the dark, the ladder leaned against the wrong side of the tree. I ought to have moved it before climbing. This seemed an especially unhelpful thing to remember. The window above the parapet belonged, according to my father’s description, to the little room where he had worked on the Ashcombe clock. He had mentioned the draught often enough. I hoped it indicated a defective catch. His notebook had been in that room for eight months. On my first request, Mr. Pritchard had said it would be looked for. On my second, he had regretted the inconvenience of my arriving during preparations for the new owner. That afternoon, he had informed me that nothing could be removed until the disputed commission was settled. “It is my father’s book,” I had said. “Precisely, Miss Vale. It may bear upon the matter.” I could have brought a solicitor into it, if I had possessed money for one. Instead I had borrowed a ladder. My skirt caught beneath my knee. I freed it, scraping my knuckles on the stone, and stood carefully. Through the glass I could see a chair, a table and the dull red remains of a fire. The window catch was indeed defective. I allowed myself a moment’s satisfaction. Then I raised the sash, climbed through, and put a wet boot squarely on the seat of an upholstered chair. “Is something wrong with the stairs?” A man stood in the inner doorway with a candlestick. I remained crouched on the chair. He wore no coat; his shirtsleeves were rolled back, and there was a dark mark on one cuff. “I beg your pardon?” “Are they being cleaned?” His gaze passed from my boot to my face. Something in his expression altered. “You are not one of the maids.” “No.” “Then perhaps you had better explain.” “Perhaps you might allow me to stand upright.” He set down the candle and moved the chair away from the table, giving me room to descend. I did so without taking his offered hand. There was nowhere inconspicuous to put my muddy feet. For several seconds we both inspected the chair. “I shall pay for cleaning it,” I said. “Let us establish who you are before opening an account.” “Clara Vale.” “The clockmaker?” “My father was Thomas Vale. I keep the shop now.” He looked towards the open window. Rain was spotting the boards. “And this is how you call upon customers?” “Only those who retain my property.” I had intended to be calm if discovered. I had also intended not to be discovered. He shut the window, testing the catch unsuccessfully. “What property?” “A brown notebook. My father left it in the workshop upstairs. Mr. Pritchard will not return it.” “This was the dressing room.” I looked at the table. Papers lay beneath a ruler, and a drawing of a doorway had been weighted flat with a cup. My father had said the second window from the end. I had counted the narrow one above the conservatory door. “You are Mr. Ashcombe,” I said. “Yes.” “Then I have written to you.” “I have your letter. Pritchard tells me the clock was never finished.” “The clock was finished in February.” “It does not go.” “Has anyone wound it?” He paused. “I cannot tell you.” “Neither can I, from here.” That was sharper than I intended. He glanced at me, and I thought he might smile, which would have been intolerable. Instead he asked what the notebook contained. “Measurements. Work done. Materials used. Other commissions besides yours. I need it.” “And you thought taking it secretly would improve your position?” “No. I thought it would give me my notebook.” He drew a breath and let it out. “The workshop is locked. Pritchard has the key.” “Where is he?” “Away until morning.” I looked at the poker. “No,” said Mr. Ashcombe. “I had not proposed anything.” “You were considering it.” He was right, which made his manner particularly disagreeable. I pulled off my wet glove. My scraped knuckles had begun to sting. “Come tomorrow at ten,” he said. “I shall have the room opened, and you can show me what was done to the clock.” “I have work tomorrow.” “So have I. Will eleven suit?” It would. I disliked having to say so. He took the candle and opened the door. I followed him down a corridor where covered furniture stood against the walls, then along a narrow staircase smelling faintly of boiled cabbage. At the bottom he lifted a latch, and cold air entered. The garden lay outside. No broken catch, no branch, no dangerous drop. I stepped onto the gravel. “Your ladder?” he asked. I had hoped to retrieve it without an audience. “By the conservatory.” He carried it as far as the gate, holding the candle awkwardly in his other hand. Once he struck a shrub with the ladder’s foot and apologized to it. I looked away before he saw my expression. At the gate he helped settle the ladder against my shoulder. “Eleven, Miss Vale.” “And the notebook will be returned?” “It belongs to you.” He said it simply. I had spent weeks trying to make someone in that house concede as much. I thanked him, though not graciously, and set off down the lane. After twenty yards I stopped to shift the ladder. He was still at the gate, the candle sheltered against his chest. Tomorrow he would ring a bell, ask for a key, and a door would open. I walked on, feeling the fresh scrape across my knuckles.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished opening chapter. The model has executed its plan with considerable skill, producing prose that feels genuinely Victorian in texture without resorting to pastiche or ornamental excess. **Voice and Style** Clara's first-person narration is immediately distinctive. The opening paragraph delivers on the plan's promise of impudence: "The difficulty lies in acquiring the first lesson without breaking one's neck." The voice is dry, self-aware, and economical. The observation "This seemed an especially unhelpful thing to remember" about the ladder placement is exactly the kind of wry, practical humor the plan called for. The narration confesses to muddy boots while maintaining dignity—precisely the balance the character profile demands. The prose avoids the twin pitfalls the plan warned against: there are no clock-and-heart metaphors, no ornamental Victorian diction. The historical texture emerges naturally through the ladder, the defective catch, the covered furniture, the boiled cabbage smell. **Dialogue** The dialogue is genuinely strong. "Is something wrong with the stairs?" is a perfect opening line for Gabriel—observational, slightly absurd, not conventionally gallant. The exchange about the poker ("No," said Mr. Ashcombe. / "I had not proposed anything." / "You were considering it.") is economical and characterful. The dialogue reveals both characters efficiently: Clara's pride, Gabriel's perceptiveness, their mutual wariness. **Character Consistency** Both characters align well with their profiles. Gabriel's visual/absurd humor (apologizing to the shrub) is exactly what the profile promised. Clara's refusal to take his hand, her sharpness about winding the clock, her reluctant gratitude—all consistent. The final image of Gabriel still at the gate with the candle is quietly effective. **Plot and Chapter Plan** The chapter follows its plan faithfully: Clara enters through the wrong window, encounters Gabriel, the disputed commission is established, the notebook is withheld (workshop locked), and an appointment is made. The ending—Clara walking away feeling the scrape on her knuckles while Gabriel has only to ring a bell—is exactly the class-consciousness the plan intended, delivered through showing rather than telling. **Minor Weaknesses** The chapter is nearly flawless in execution, but a few small observations: The transition from the parapet to the interior is slightly rushed—we don't quite feel the physical difficulty of the climb itself. The line "He said it simply. I had spent weeks trying to make someone in that house concede as much." edges toward telling rather than showing, though it's brief and earns its place. The "apologized to it" moment (shrub) is charming but could be seen as slightly too cute—though it fits the character profile precisely. **Creativity and Surprise** The chapter avoids the predictable meet-cute. Gabriel's assumption that she's a servant, his practical response to the situation, the absence of romantic gallantry—these are genuinely fresh choices. The ending resists sentimentality while still being emotionally resonant. **Overall Assessment** This is high-quality literary fiction executing a well-conceived plan with precision and restraint. The voice is consistent, the characters are alive, the dialogue earns its keep, and the historical texture is worn lightly. It reads like the work of a skilled author who has thought carefully about what the story needs. # Chapter 2 — Thirty-Eight Pounds At eleven the following morning, I was shown into a passage beside the kitchen and asked to wait. I had worn my better gloves. The left concealed my scraped knuckles; the right had a small split which I kept turned towards my skirt. Through an open door, a woman was explaining that six eggs had been ordered, not eight, and that breaking two would not improve the arithmetic. Mr. Ashcombe appeared before I could hear the answer. “Miss Vale. I thought you had not arrived.” “I was put here.” He glanced at the chair beneath the row of bells. “Come through.” There was no rebuke to the maid who had admitted me. I was grateful; I did not want an enemy in the kitchen before luncheon. Mr. Pritchard waited in the gallery. He had supervised my father’s work, approved his access to the house, and offered him refreshment on at least three occasions. Now he inclined his head with the air of receiving an unfamiliar applicant. “Miss Vale.” “Mr. Pritchard.” The clock stood between two long windows. Its walnut case was handsome enough, though somebody had set a porcelain shepherdess on top of it. I put down my bag. “May I?” Mr. Ashcombe nodded. I moved the shepherdess to a table. One china slipper had been mended badly. “The clock, I believe, is our concern,” said Pritchard. “It is mine.” I opened the case. My father had replaced worn pivot holes and repaired damage to the striking mechanism. I knew the work because I had helped him prepare the replacement parts. He had brought the smaller assemblies home wrapped in an old flannel shirt. I examined what I could without dismantling anything. Then I took out my winding key. “The key is in the drawer,” Pritchard said. “I have one.” The weights had reached the bottom. I wound the clock, set the pendulum moving, and listened. It ran for nearly a minute before faltering. Pritchard shifted beside me. “The old oil has thickened,” I said. “It needs cleaning. When was it last attended to?” “Your father undertook to put it in order.” “He did. In February. Has anyone wound it regularly since?” Nobody answered. Mr. Ashcombe bent to look inside. I moved aside, although he could learn little from staring. “Can you establish whether the repair was completed?” he asked. “Yes. The repaired parts are sound. I can show you, if you wish.” “I wish,” he said. Pritchard remained standing while I explained. He looked neither at the bearing I indicated nor at the section my father had repaired. When Mr. Ashcombe asked a question, it was at least about the mechanism. We went upstairs afterwards. The workshop was the next room along from the one I had entered. Its window stood conveniently above a broad stretch of conservatory roof. I looked at it longer than necessary. Pritchard unlocked a cupboard. My father’s notebook lay beside a broken wooden packing case. I recognized the pale mark where he had once rested a cup on its cover. Taking it from Pritchard, I had the absurd impression that it ought to be warm. There were entries for customers I had forgotten, a calculation crossed out three times, and a reminder to buy me new tweezers. I turned past that page quickly. The Ashcombe commission occupied six pages. At the end, beneath my father’s account of the work, another hand had written: *Examined and approved. H. Ashcombe.* Mr. Ashcombe took the book when I offered it. “That is his signature.” “There may have been subsequent difficulties,” Pritchard said. “There may,” I answered. “What were they?” “I cannot be expected to recall every conversation.” “Yet you recalled enough to say the work was unfinished.” Mr. Ashcombe was reading the next line. “Payment deferred until Michaelmas by agreement.” “My father’s agreement,” I said. He had come home pleased with himself that evening. I remembered now. Mr. Ashcombe had been most appreciative. There would be other work. Michaelmas had passed while my father lay dying. Pritchard straightened his cuffs. “Then we appear to have suffered an administrative confusion.” I held out my hand for the notebook. “How much is owing?” Mr. Ashcombe asked. “Thirty-eight pounds.” He glanced at Pritchard, who said nothing. “The estate cannot conveniently meet every outstanding account at once.” “Nor can my shop.” “No,” he said. “I see that.” I doubted he did. He was trying, which was not quite the same thing. We settled on ten pounds that day and the remainder within a month. I asked for the arrangement in writing. Pritchard supplied paper with such deliberation that I wondered whether its cost would be deducted. “And the statement that the work was defective must be corrected,” I said. “It has reached people who buy from me.” “Who?” asked Mr. Ashcombe. “One customer mentioned it. I suspect others have heard.” “Find out what was said. We shall address it.” I wanted something firmer, but I had my book and a payment promised. For that morning I let it stand. He commissioned the cleaning separately. I named my charge before Pritchard could suggest it belonged to the previous bill. On the stairs, Mr. Ashcombe stopped beneath an elaborate carved bracket. “Mind this.” He immediately struck his head against it. I made a noise which I hoped resembled concern. “It serves no purpose,” he said, rubbing his temple. “It appears to support the shelf.” “The shelf serves no purpose either.” He examined the fastening, then glanced at my bag. “Have you a screwdriver?” “Not one suitable for that.” A minute later he returned with his own. I watched him loosen the bracket, one hand braced against its grotesque wooden face. “My cousin called this an improvement.” “Perhaps he was shorter.” He laughed. The bracket came free unexpectedly, and he caught it against his waistcoat. I laughed then too, without intending to. For a moment we stood together on the stairs, pleased by something that had nothing to do with thirty-eight pounds.

# Chapter 3 — After the Lamps Are Lit By Wednesday afternoon, the clock was running and I had acquired a dislike of the gallery’s second window. It faced west, but a stone ornament outside intercepted the light precisely where I needed it. I had moved my chair twice before Mr. Ashcombe found me carrying the table. “Let me.” “Take that end, then. Mind the tray.” He looked down at the parts arranged on a cloth and approached with care. We shifted the table three feet. “Better?” he asked. “Until the sun moves.” “I have been considering removing the stonework.” “Then consider it favourably.” He went to the window. “My cousin had it copied from a house in Italy. I suspect the original had more sun to spare.” He had brought drawings. I supposed he wanted my approval for something, now that we had successfully collaborated on the removal of a bracket. His proposal involved enlarging the morning-room windows. “You will lose that cupboard,” I said. “Yes.” “Where will its contents go?” “Somewhere else.” I looked at him. “I shall consult Mrs. Finch,” he added. He spread another sheet on the table, safely beyond my tools. This showed the morning room as it was, including a small chair beside the hearth. “Why have you drawn the chair?” “It was there.” “It needn’t have been.” “No. But I liked it.” I understood that better than I expected to. He stayed while I reassembled the striking work. At first he asked questions. Then, apparently discovering that I answered less agreeably when interrupted, he sat with his drawings and allowed me to forget him. When I looked up, he was watching my hands. “What?” “Nothing. You stopped moving your lips.” “I beg your pardon?” “You were counting, I think.” I had been. I wished he had noticed something more impressive. The clock struck four correctly, with sufficient force to end the conversation. Mr. Ashcombe stood. “I have some drawings upstairs you might prefer. Buildings with cupboards left intact.” “I shall inspect them another time.” “This evening, perhaps. After dinner.” He looked at my bag, already fastened, and then towards the open gallery door. “I mean—Mrs. Finch could—” “Supervise the cupboards?” “That was not what I was going to say.” But whatever he had meant to say had deserted him. I put on my gloves. The sensible arrangement would have been tomorrow afternoon, or Friday. There was nothing about architectural drawings that required darkness. “The workshop window is more conveniently situated than yours,” I said. He watched me fasten a button. “So I discovered.” “Does its catch work?” “Yes.” “A pity.” I ought to have stopped there. He ought to have laughed and shown me out. Instead he said, “It need not be fastened.” *** I spent the walk home finding objections. The roof would be wet. Someone might see me. I had no reason to examine drawings after dinner when I had been perfectly free to examine them before it. By the time I reached the shop, I had decided not to go. At half past eight I was standing beneath the conservatory. This time I had placed the ladder correctly. The workshop window rose quietly, and Mr. Ashcombe looked up from arranging papers beneath two candlesticks. “You came.” “You left it open.” “Yes.” Neither of us improved upon this exchange. He moved aside while I climbed in. I had brought an old cloth to wipe my boots, which seemed a modest contribution towards respectability. The room was cold. Mr. Ashcombe had lit a fire, but it was still considering whether to burn. “I thought it would be warmer by now.” “Have you opened the damper?” He looked at the fireplace. I took off my coat and opened it. His refreshments consisted of a decanter, two glasses and four biscuits on a plate. The biscuits looked as though they had been obtained secretly. “I was not sure what you would like.” “Neither am I.” He poured me a little sherry. I tasted it and discovered that I liked it very much. The drawings were not proposals for Ashcombe. One showed a narrow London house divided into floors, with annotations so small I bent close to read them. “You drew all this?” “Most of it. My employer corrected the staircase.” “Why?” “Because mine would have delivered a tall man into a beam.” “That seems a recurring difficulty.” He smiled. There were measurements, estimates, alterations made in another hand. These interested me more than the graceful finished elevations. Somebody had argued in pencil about the position of a drain. “I thought architects designed churches.” “Some do. I spent a considerable part of last year persuading a merchant that his servants required somewhere to sleep.” “Did you succeed?” “We compromised. They acquired beds; he retained the larger wine cellar.” He spoke of the office without making it sound either miserable or distinguished. There had been bad tea, an unreliable stove, a senior draughtsman who whistled the same six bars every afternoon. “You miss it,” I said. “Yes.” “Will you go back?” “I don’t know how much of my time this place intends to consume.” The fire settled with a small collapse. He glanced towards it, then at me. I told him about a customer who wound his watch with kitchen tongs after losing the key. It was not an equivalent confidence, but he laughed and asked what had become of the watch. We talked until the gallery clock struck ten. I reached for my coat too quickly, catching its sleeve beneath the biscuit plate. He caught the plate. One biscuit fell. We left it where it landed. At the window, I gathered my skirts and looked down. The ladder stood exactly where it should. “Will it be unlatched on Thursday?” I asked. He answered before I could pretend to mean anything else. “Yes.” I descended carefully. On the walk home, my sensible objections returned, accompanied now by the precise recollection of his face when he had said it.

# Chapter 4 — Thursday On Thursday I caught my heel in the hem of my skirt and nearly left a shoe on the conservatory roof. Mr. Ashcombe, who had been watching my arrival from the window, laughed. “Do not,” I said. “I’m sorry.” “You are not.” “No. Give me your hand.” “Wait.” The buckle had caught a loop of thread. I could either pull and tear my hem or stand upon one foot until he stopped finding me amusing. He leaned out, holding the sash above my head. “You might sit on the sill.” “I might have stayed at home.” Nevertheless, I sat. He kept hold of the window while I freed myself, and only laughed again when I was safely inside. I ought to have minded more. There was a proper fire this time. My cloth lay folded beside the window, where I had forgotten it the previous evening. Seeing it waiting for me produced an unreasonable feeling of having been expected for years. “I have brought something,” he said. “I hope it is a chair for the conservatory roof.” He showed me a drawing of a monument: a marble urn beneath a drooping stone cloth, supported by two creatures with wings and unhappy human faces. “Your predecessor’s latest improvement?” “His grandfather’s. It stands in the church.” I recognized it. My father had once taken me to Ashcombe church to measure the space beside the organ for a proposed clock. Nothing had come of the commission. I had remembered the winged creatures, which appeared to be suffering from toothache. Gabriel unfolded a smaller sheet. “I copied the inscription.” “Why?” “I thought you might appreciate it.” He read aloud with considerable gravity. “‘Distinguished alike by the sweetness of his domestic affections and the unbending firmness of his public principles.’” “I should not have liked to ask him for anything.” “There is more.” “There would be.” We examined the drawing together. One creature had a wing raised at an angle that made its burden seem particularly uncomfortable. “Was he a good man?” I asked. “I don’t know. He opposed a new road across the estate.” “Perhaps that was the firmness.” “Perhaps.” We had stopped laughing. I wondered who had chosen the words, and whether they had believed them. Gabriel folded the inscription. “My cousin spoke well of him.” “My father spoke well of your cousin.” The words had come out more sharply than I intended. Gabriel looked up. “He was generous to people he liked.” “Yes,” I said. “I believe my father liked being liked.” I moved closer to the fire and held out my hands. “He would come home with promises of further work as though they were money. Sometimes there was further work. Sometimes there was only another promise.” “That must have been trying.” “It was. He gave people time we could not afford.” “Then you must find it a relief to have the accounts to yourself.” I turned. He was still smiling a little. It disappeared. “I meant the business.” “So did I.” “No. I don’t think I—” I looked back at the fire. There was nothing false in what he had said. That was partly why I could not bear it. Behind me, paper rustled. Then it stopped. “My father died in debt,” he said. I waited, unwilling to help him. “I remember being angry about a tailor’s bill. It seemed an indecent thing to be angry about, that week.” “Were you?” “Yes.” “Then I wish you had said that first.” “So do I.” For a while we stood without speaking. A coal shifted against the grate. At last he asked, “May I pour you some sherry?” “A little.” He gave me the glass without looking anxious for forgiveness, which helped. I sat beside the table. He remained standing until I moved his drawings from the other chair. We talked about something else. I cannot remember what began it. I remember disagreeing with him about the value of a south-facing workshop, and his admitting that he disliked rising early enough to judge an eastern light. “I had supposed you industrious,” I said. “I hoped you might.” He was close enough now that I could see where he had nicked his chin shaving. I wanted to touch it. The desire was so particular and so foolish that I looked down at my glass. “Clara.” It was the first time he had used my name. I put the glass on the table. He bent towards me slowly enough that I might have turned away. I did not. The kiss was brief. Afterwards, he drew back only a little, and I found myself looking at his mouth. “That was—” he began. “Please do not describe it.” He laughed under his breath. I caught his sleeve and kissed him again. A knock sounded at the door. We separated so abruptly that my chair scraped the boards. Mrs. Finch entered carrying two folded towels. “Forgive me, sir. I understood these rooms were empty.” Her eyes went to my coat, then to the open curtains. “No,” Gabriel said unnecessarily. “I see that.” She placed the towels in a cupboard. I stood, although there was no reason to. Gabriel began saying something about the drawings. Mrs. Finch listened without assisting him. “I shall leave you to them, sir.” “I was going,” I said. “I will show you down.” Neither Gabriel nor I objected. At the turn of the stairs she waited for me to catch up. Her hand rested firmly on the banister. “I am not asking what you were doing upstairs, Miss Vale.” I said nothing. “But that roof is visible from Mr. Pritchard’s sitting room.” Through the passage window I could see a rectangle of light across the courtyard. Mrs. Finch opened the side door. “Good night.” I stepped outside, holding my coat closed. There was still a ladder beneath the conservatory, and I had to go back for it.

# Chapter 5 — An Amicable Settlement The letter arrived on Saturday, wrapped around an invoice for materials I had ordered before Michaelmas. Hobson & Reed regretted that they could no longer extend the usual terms. Future orders would require payment in advance. Below this, in Mr. Hobson’s smaller hand, was a sentence evidently intended as kindness. *You will appreciate that Mr. Pritchard’s account of the difficulties at Ashcombe gives us cause for caution, particularly under the altered management of your business.* I read “altered management” three times. Then I fetched my father’s notebook, put both documents in my bag, and walked to the manor. I did not change my gloves. Gabriel received me in the room I had first entered through the window. The chair had been cleaned. I noticed this before I noticed how carefully he greeted me. “Miss Vale.” “Mr. Ashcombe.” He shut the door. “I was going to write.” “I have brought something for you to read.” He took the letter. As he read, his thumb moved along the edge of the paper, bending it slightly. “I wondered where the report had originated,” he said. “Now we know.” “Yes.” He returned to the beginning and read it again. “Has Mr. Pritchard seen it?” I asked. “Not this letter. I spoke to him yesterday about the account.” “And?” “He maintains that there was uncertainty about the work.” “He was present when you examined it.” “I know.” He put the letter down with unnecessary care. “He also had something to say about your visits.” The room seemed to become smaller. “What?” “Nothing I intend to repeat.” “You need not spare me his language.” “I am sparing you his insinuations.” I sat down because standing had begun to feel like waiting for a dismissal. Gabriel remained beside the table. “He suggested that I could no longer consider your claim impartially.” “Did you require impartiality to read your cousin’s signature?” “No.” “Then what has Thursday to do with thirty-eight pounds?” “Nothing. I told him so.” Yet he looked embarrassed, and I could not tell how much of that embarrassment belonged to me. He opened a drawer. “The ten pounds is ready. I apologize that you have had to ask for it.” I had not asked. Until that moment I had forgotten it. He laid a folded packet on the table, followed by a sheet of paper. “I can pay the balance myself. Immediately. There is no reason you should wait upon the estate’s difficulties.” “And Mr. Hobson?” “I propose sending this.” The letter was addressed to Hobson & Reed. It stated that the account between Ashcombe and Vale had been amicably settled and that Gabriel trusted their previous commercial arrangements might continue. I reached the end and looked for another page. “There is nothing here about the work.” “It establishes that there is no outstanding dispute.” “There was a dispute because your steward said my father had not done what he charged for.” “And I am offering to settle it.” “With whose money?” “Mine.” “The debt is the estate’s.” “Yes, Clara. I understand the distinction.” He spoke patiently. That was worse than impatience. I laid the letter down. “Mr. Hobson will suppose you have paid a doubtful bill out of kindness. He may be grateful to you for rescuing an unfortunate young woman.” “I cannot govern everything he chooses to suppose.” “You could tell him what happened.” “I am trying to prevent this becoming a public quarrel.” “It became public when Pritchard answered a private inquiry with a lie.” Gabriel moved towards the fireplace, then stopped. “There are other people involved. Other accounts. I need to establish what has been done before making accusations.” “Then establish it. But you know what was done to mine.” He looked tired. I had liked that face two nights earlier, when the firelight caught the hollow beneath his cheekbone. I resented remembering it now. “The bill would be paid,” he said. “Your supplier would have my assurance. What practical purpose is served by forcing Pritchard to humiliate himself?” “I did not ask him to kneel.” “You are refusing a solution because it does not provide a public victory.” For a moment I could not answer. He regretted the words; I saw it. But he also believed them. “A victory,” I repeated. “That was badly expressed.” “How should it have been expressed?” He rubbed his forehead. “I don’t know.” I picked up the packet containing the ten pounds. “This is due under our agreement?” “Yes.” “I shall send a receipt.” “You needn’t—” “I shall send one.” There was no dignity in leaving earned money on his table. I needed to pay Mr. Hobson, whether Gabriel found me mercenary or not. I put the packet in my bag. “The balance may come when we agreed. I do not want your private money.” “It was not meant as charity.” “What was it meant as?” “Help.” “You want an inexpensive conscience and a woman willing to keep using the window.” He stepped back as though I had struck him. I knew the second accusation was unfair. I had proposed the window. I had asked about Thursday. I let it stand. “Do not send that letter,” I said. “Clara.” “There will be no more evening visits.” “I gathered that.” His anger steadied me more than his patience had. I took Mr. Hobson’s letter and my notebook from the table. At the door, the fastening of my bag caught. I struggled with it while Gabriel watched. “Do you believe,” he asked, “that everything between us was a deception?” I could have said no. It was the true answer. But he might have come towards me then, and I was afraid of wanting him to. I opened the door and left.

# Chapter 6 — A Letter in Her Own Name I spoiled two sheets of paper before writing a letter Mr. Hobson could answer without first forgiving me. The first began, “Your willingness to accept an unsupported allegation.” The second was worse. I folded both into small squares and put them beneath the short leg of the table. At least they would be useful. Then I copied the acknowledgment from my father’s notebook, keeping the wording and date exact. I explained that the repair had been examined by the present Mr. Ashcombe, who had acknowledged the debt. I enclosed payment for a smaller order of materials than I had originally requested. There was a watch waiting for a new mainspring. Its owner had already called twice. I could postpone buying other things, but not that. I counted the remaining money. Ten pounds looked substantial in a gentleman’s study. Divided between an invoice, the rent and three weeks of household expenses, it became a collection of inadequate little sums. Upstairs, my father’s coat still hung beside the kitchen door. I took it down while the kettle boiled. Something hard struck the floor. It was a watch key, larger than any I regularly used, attached to a piece of faded ribbon. He had tied ribbon to things he was always losing, then lost the ribbon with them. I picked it up and sat with the coat across my knees. He would have liked Gabriel. That troubled me more than the money for several minutes. When the kettle boiled over, I got up. *** Mrs. Finch came on Tuesday afternoon to collect a small clock from the servants’ hall. Its alarm had ceased to function. She had brought it herself a fortnight earlier, explaining that punctuality ought not to depend upon the kitchen maid waking naturally. I was fitting the watch spring when the shop bell sounded. “One moment, please.” She waited without touching anything. Customers frequently examined the objects on the counter as though I kept them there to invite opinions. When I had secured the spring, I fetched her clock from the shelf. “The alarm is set for five,” I said. “I have tested it.” “Good. Alice claims she cannot hear the ordinary striking.” “Perhaps she cannot.” Mrs. Finch looked at me. “I have heard Alice complain about a mouse behind the skirting.” I wound the alarm and demonstrated the setting. She watched closely, then repeated the adjustment herself. “What do I owe you?” I gave her the bill. She opened her purse. “The household account will do,” I said, before remembering. Her hand stopped. “No,” I added. “Forgive me. That was habit.” “There is nothing to forgive.” She counted the money onto the counter. Neither of us referred to whose habit it had been. I wrapped the clock in the cloth she had brought. She continued standing there after it was ready. “Mr. Ashcombe has been asking questions,” she said. “About the clocks?” “About the bills.” I folded one corner over the handle. “I hope he receives answers.” “He has received mine.” There was enough in her tone to make me look up. “I knew some accounts were delayed,” she said. “Food comes every day. Coal must be ordered. There have been choices.” “My supplier has choices too.” “Yes.” She removed one glove, finger by finger. The skin beneath was red where the seams had pressed. “I did not know what Mr. Pritchard had said about your father.” “But you knew he was not being paid.” “I knew several people were not being paid.” She spoke without emphasis. I had wanted an admission; now I had one, it gave me less satisfaction than expected. “There are eleven people to be paid on Friday,” she said. “If wages are short, they come to me. Not to Mr. Pritchard.” “What am I supposed to do with that?” “I don’t know, Miss Vale. But you spoke as though I had been protecting a cupboard of silver.” I looked towards the drawer where I kept my accounts. “No,” I said eventually. “I suppose you weren’t.” Her glove lay between us, carefully flattened. “When my husband died, there were wages owing to him. I received them after nine weeks. The lady of the house sent me a shawl.” “Did you keep it?” “It was a good shawl.” I smiled reluctantly. “I would have preferred the wages.” “So would I.” She pulled on her glove. I wanted to ask whether Gabriel had spoken of me, then became angry with myself for wanting it. Mrs. Finch lifted the clock. “The roof was foolish,” she said. “I have discovered several people can see it.” “That was not my only objection.” “I did not imagine it was.” For the first time, she looked tired rather than stern. She shifted the bundle to her other arm. I opened the door for her. “Mind the step.” “I saw it.” She descended carefully. *** Gabriel’s note arrived the next morning with the carrier who brought parcels from the manor into town. There were five lines. He asked whether I would attend a meeting on Friday at eleven concerning the statement made to Hobson & Reed. Pritchard and Mrs. Finch would be present. He wished me to bring the supplier’s letter and my father’s notebook. There was no enclosure beyond his visiting card, apparently added to provide the address I knew perfectly well. I turned it over. The back was blank. Then I read the note again, making myself attend to what it said rather than what it did not say. A meeting could accomplish very little. I had attended several conversations with Pritchard already, though perhaps they had lacked the necessary number of chairs. I wrote that I would come. Before sealing my answer, I nearly added a sentence about Saturday. I had found several better ways of conducting that argument during the hours since leaving his study. Instead I addressed the envelope. The repaired watch was ticking beside my elbow. I carried it to the window to examine the dial, where the light was better.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a quietly accomplished piece of character-driven fiction that largely succeeds on its own terms. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. **Voice and Narration** Clara's first-person voice is consistently maintained throughout. The opening gambit—spoiling two sheets of paper, folding them under the table leg—is economical and characterful. It shows her practicality, her anger, and her dark humor without announcing any of these qualities. The line "At least they would be useful" is exactly the kind of dry, self-aware observation the plan promised. The voice never becomes precious or over-literary; it stays grounded in the material world of invoices, mainsprings, and watch keys. **The Watch Key Scene** The discovery of the watch key in her father's coat is the chapter's most emotionally resonant moment, and it's handled with admirable restraint. "He had tied ribbon to things he was always losing, then lost the ribbon with them" is a beautifully specific detail that earns its emotional weight. The follow-up—"He would have liked Gabriel. That troubled me more than the money for several minutes"—is a small masterpiece of compressed feeling. It reveals Clara's emotional state without explaining it, trusts the reader, and the kettle boiling over provides a perfectly timed interruption that prevents sentimentality. This is the chapter's best passage. **The Mrs. Finch Scene** This is the chapter's longest and most complex scene, and it mostly succeeds. The exchange about Alice and the mouse is a nice piece of characterization that establishes Mrs. Finch's practical intelligence before the harder conversation begins. The dialogue is well-calibrated: both women speak obliquely, neither fully capitulates, and the conversation ends in something like mutual respect without false warmth. The detail of Mrs. Finch removing her glove "finger by finger" and the red skin beneath is good physical grounding. The exchange about the shawl is particularly effective—it gives Mrs. Finch a personal history that illuminates her position without turning her into a symbol, and Clara's question "Did you keep it?" is exactly the right response: curious, slightly deflecting, and revealing of her own character. The line "It was a good shawl" followed by "I would have preferred the wages" / "So would I" is the chapter's best dialogue exchange—economical, character-revealing, and genuinely moving. However, there are moments where the scene becomes slightly schematic. Mrs. Finch's speech about eleven people being paid on Friday is taken almost verbatim from the character profile's voice experiments, which gives it a slightly rehearsed quality. The line "you spoke as though I had been protecting a cupboard of silver" is good, but Clara's response—"No. I suppose you weren't"—resolves the tension perhaps a touch too neatly. The plan called for neither woman to leave "entirely satisfied," and this is achieved, but the emotional resolution feels slightly more complete than the plan intended. **Gabriel's Note** The final section is handled with characteristic restraint. The detail of the visiting card "apparently added to provide the address I knew perfectly well" is a nice touch—it reveals Gabriel's awkwardness without stating it. Clara's near-addition of a sentence about Saturday, then her decision against it, is psychologically true. The ending—carrying the watch to the window for better light—is a good closing image: practical, slightly deflecting, and consistent with Clara's character. **Following the Chapter Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely. The letter to Hobson is written; the cost of the dispute is exposed through concrete financial detail; Mrs. Finch visits and their conversation is appropriately uneasy; Clara does not offer easy reassurance; Gabriel's note arrives and Clara agrees to come while remaining uncertain of his motives. The plan's note that "Clara also recognizes that her father's habit of informal generosity is one business practice she will not preserve" is handled through the moment where she instinctively offers the household account, then catches herself—this is shown rather than stated, which is the right choice. **Weaknesses** The chapter is somewhat low on dramatic tension. It's a transitional chapter by design, but the Mrs. Finch scene, while well-written, occasionally feels like two characters exchanging positions rather than genuinely surprising each other. The line "I had wanted an admission; now I had one, it gave me less satisfaction than expected" is slightly too explicit—it tells us what the scene has already shown. This is a minor instance of tell-don't-show in an otherwise show-heavy chapter. The prose is clean and controlled throughout, with no purple passages or forced metaphors. The historical texture is present but unobtrusive—the watch spring, the carrier from the manor, the coal ordering—all feel natural rather than decorative. **Overall Assessment** This is a confident, controlled chapter that serves its transitional function well. It doesn't attempt to do more than it should, which is itself a form of craft. The emotional beats are earned, the dialogue is largely excellent, and the voice is consistent. Its weaknesses are minor: occasional over-explicitness, one slightly schematic exchange, and a resolution to the Mrs. Finch scene that's marginally too tidy. But these are small complaints against a chapter that consistently delivers on its promises. # Chapter 7 — The Correction There were four chairs arranged around the table. I was ashamed of feeling relieved that they were all alike. Pritchard stood beside the fireplace. Mrs. Finch sat with her gloves folded in her lap, looking as though she had left something important unattended. Gabriel came forward when I entered. “Thank you for coming.” I gave him Mr. Hobson’s letter. He did not ask whether I had received his note, or comment upon the weather. For this I was grateful. “Please sit down.” Pritchard waited until Gabriel took his chair. The window through which I had first entered was closed. Someone had mended the catch. I put my bag on the floor and looked at the table instead. Gabriel passed the supplier’s letter to Pritchard. “Is this an accurate account of what you told Mr. Hobson?” Pritchard read it slowly. “I cannot answer for the construction he has placed upon our conversation.” “What did you tell him?” “That there had been difficulties with the commission. As there had.” “Difficulties with payment,” I said. Pritchard glanced at me, then back at Gabriel. “At the time, the condition of the work was in question.” “Who questioned it?” Gabriel asked. “The clock had stopped.” “After months without maintenance. You heard Miss Vale’s explanation.” “I was referring to the earlier conversation.” I opened the notebook at the marked page and laid it beside the letter. “My father left this in your keeping.” “In the workshop.” “You knew where it was.” “I cannot be expected to examine every notebook a tradesman leaves behind.” “You examined it sufficiently to refuse to return it.” Gabriel looked at him. Pritchard’s lips tightened. “I considered it relevant to an unsettled account.” “It was,” I said. Nobody spoke for a moment. From the passage came the faint clatter of something being carried on a tray. Gabriel turned the notebook so that Pritchard could read the acknowledgment. “Did you know my cousin had approved the work?” “Yes. Initially.” “Was it subsequently rejected?” “There were verbal discussions.” “With whom?” “Your cousin.” “Concerning the quality of the repair?” Pritchard looked down at the page. “Concerning the expense.” Mrs. Finch moved her gloves from one knee to the other. Gabriel leaned back. “That is a different matter.” “Not when one is required to find the money, sir.” It was the first thing Pritchard had said without qualification. “Your cousin expected the household to continue as before. He did not wish the stables reduced. He would not postpone the work on the south roof. There were instructions to accommodate him.” “By withholding payment?” “By making arrangements.” “My father made one,” I said. “You have it there.” “And others would make none. If you wish to examine these accounts separately, sir, you must also examine what the money paid for.” “I have begun.” Pritchard looked up sharply. Gabriel drew a paper towards him. “My cousin authorized work he could not afford. You concealed the unpaid bills among disputed accounts. I accepted your explanation because it was easier than discovering how little money there was.” “Sir—” “Mr. Bell will examine the books on Monday. Until he has done so, you will not authorize or withhold payments.” Mrs. Finch spoke. “Friday’s wages?” “Are provided for. I shall see you afterwards.” She nodded, but did not look reassured. Gabriel handed me the paper. “This concerns your account.” The correction was short. It named my father, the work, the date of approval and the debt. It stated that the allegation of defective workmanship was unfounded and should not have been made. I read it twice. “Has Mr. Hobson received this?” “Not yet. I wanted you to see it first.” There was no assurance of amicable settlement. No request that anyone indulge me. I nodded. “Who else received such an account?” Gabriel asked Pritchard. “I should have to consult my correspondence.” “Please do. Include anyone to whom you spoke.” Pritchard began aligning the supplier’s letter with the edge of the notebook. I reached across and took both. “Will that be all, sir?” “For now.” He left before Mrs. Finch. She paused beside my chair. “Your clock woke Alice this morning.” “Did she get up?” “Eventually.” Then she followed him out. Gabriel remained seated. I watched the door close. I had imagined relief as something warmer. Instead I felt emptied and faintly sick. “You may keep that copy,” he said. His signature occupied less space than my father’s acknowledgment. It would probably accomplish more than my letters and explanations together. “Thank you.” He looked at his hands. “I should have done this when you first brought the letter.” “Yes.” “I thought, with what Pritchard had seen, that a public disagreement might expose you to—” “Must we begin there again?” He stopped. Outside, wheels sounded on the gravel. We listened until they had passed. “I was ashamed,” he said. I looked at him. “Of my own judgment being questioned. I wished you would accept the money and allow me to stop feeling ashamed.” I folded the correction carefully. “That was not all you wished.” “No. But it was enough to make me behave badly.” I put the paper in my bag. There were things I might have said about the window. I could not yet find a way to say them without reopening the whole argument. At the door, Gabriel asked whether he might visit the shop. “On business?” “No.” I kept my hand on the latch. “I cannot promise to be agreeable.” “I remember.” Against my wishes, I nearly smiled. “Thursday afternoon. After three.” “Thank you.” I left before either of us could improve upon the arrangement. In the passage, Mrs. Finch was directing two men carrying a carpet. I waited against the wall while they struggled past, then made my own way out through the front door.

# Chapter 8 — During Business Hours Gabriel’s first visit lasted seventeen minutes. I know because he arrived while I was testing a watch and left when its owner came to collect it. We discussed the rain, Mrs. Finch’s alarm clock and a loose tile above my doorway. He did not offer to repair the tile. I did not invite him upstairs. Afterwards, I wished he had stayed. The next Thursday he brought the drawing I had admired, rolled loosely and tied with string. “You need not hang it,” he said. “I have not decided whether to accept it.” He looked so disconcerted that I took pity on him. “Leave it there. Away from the oil.” It hung above the kitchen table by Sunday. *** The balance of the manor’s account arrived on the promised date. I entered the payment in the ledger, ruled a line beneath it, and sat for some time with my pen uncapped. There was no reason to leave the page open. I closed the book. Mr. Hobson wrote to express satisfaction that the matter had been clarified. He offered me thirty days’ credit, rather than the sixty my father had enjoyed. I accepted. A customer who had removed his watch from my care sent it back by his gardener without explanation. Another never returned. Pritchard remained at Ashcombe while the accounts were examined, but no longer answered inquiries from tradesmen. Gabriel spoke little of him. Once, while waiting for me to finish a repair, he unfolded a letter and read it with an expression that discouraged questions. “How bad?” I asked. He refolded it. “Manageable, if nothing else requires a roof.” “That seems unlikely in England.” “Yes.” He looked tired. I put the kettle on. *** By November he had learned which chair did not wobble and where he could place his hat without obstructing my work. He still sometimes asked questions when I was counting. On the afternoon he brought his watch, I was replacing the glass in a cheap little timepiece whose owner had warned me three times against scratching it. Gabriel stood at the counter until I looked up. “It loses seven minutes a day.” “Since when?” “Last week.” “And you have waited until Thursday?” “I knew you would be here.” “I am generally here.” “Yes,” he said. “I have noticed.” I took the watch. It was plain, good quality, and warmer than the shop. He sat while I finished fitting the glass. Outside, somebody was calling for a dog with increasing personal resentment. Gabriel’s watch had been dropped. “Not recently,” he said. “How long ago?” “Before Michaelmas.” I looked at him. “It was going afterwards.” “Badly.” “Only recently.” I opened the case and bent over it. He waited. That was one of the things I had come to like: once he settled, he could be quiet without making me feel responsible for his entertainment. After a while he said, “Clara.” “Mm?” “I should like to marry you.” My tweezers remained suspended above the movement. “Put those down first,” he added. I did, though not because he had told me to. He had risen from his chair. There was something almost apologetic in the way he stood, as though he had brought a much larger object into the shop than it could accommodate. “Have you been waiting all afternoon to say that?” “Yes.” “You might have mentioned it before giving me your watch.” “I wanted you to look at the watch.” I laughed then, unexpectedly, and covered my mouth. His expression changed enough to make me lower my hand. “I am not laughing at the proposal.” “I hoped not.” “Yes,” I said. He came towards me, but I put my hand on the counter between us. “Wait. Where should we live?” He stopped. “At Ashcombe, I supposed.” “And the shop?” “I thought you would keep it.” “From three miles away?” “There could be a carriage.” “Every morning?” “If you wished.” I pictured myself descending from a carriage while a customer stood waiting outside my locked door. “I begin early.” “I know.” “You cannot know how early. You arrive after luncheon.” He looked at the counter. “I had thought of having rooms made suitable for your work.” “At the manor?” “Yes.” “Gabriel, people bring me clocks in baskets. They will not wish to call at Ashcombe.” “I meant it as a possibility.” “You meant it as an arrangement.” He opened his mouth, then shut it. Beyond the window, the man had found his dog. Their reunion sounded unhappy. “I don’t know,” Gabriel said at last. “I had got as far as hoping you would say yes.” I looked down at his watch, lying open beside my tools. “We need not decide this afternoon.” “No.” “But you must not order benches.” “I shall refrain from ordering benches.” I moved my hand from the counter. He took it, carefully avoiding the sore place at the base of my thumb. I had not imagined marriage in this shop, with a customer’s scratched brass case beneath my elbow and tomorrow’s repairs waiting in their envelopes. Yet I could hardly imagine discussing it anywhere else. His thumb rested against my wrist. “You did say yes?” “Yes.” He bent towards me. “Not yet.” This time he looked genuinely alarmed. I withdrew my hand, went to the door and turned the sign. Then I pulled down the blind and returned to him. *** It was nearly dark when he left. I had lit the lamp twice; the first match went out while he was kissing me. At the door he remembered his watch. “I shall keep it,” I said. “For repair?” “What else?” He smiled, then glanced back at the bench. “May I come tomorrow?” “The shop opens at eight.” “Are you very strict about your hours?” “For customers.” “I see.” “And use the door.” He looked up towards the rooms above us. “I have no ladder.” “I shall lend you one,” I said, and kissed him good night.

Clara's pride, her precision, her enjoyment of outwitting expectations, her practical romanticism — all present. Gabriel's tendency toward premature arrangements (the carriage, the rooms at the manor), his ability to be corrected without losing dignity, his patience — all present. This is a chapter that achieves what the plan set out to do: an unmistakable romantic commitment without instant prosperity or universal acceptance, rendered through specific, particular, character-revealing action and dialogue. Final Piece Evaluation

Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of Victorian romantic fiction. The author has constructed a coherent, character-driven narrative across eight chapters with impressive consistency and craft. Let me examine it critically across the relevant dimensions. **Strengths:** The dialogue is the story's greatest achievement. It is sharp, economical, and character-revealing without ever becoming expository. Lines like "Is something wrong with the stairs?" and the exchange about the bracket ("It serves no purpose." / "It appears to support the shelf." / "The shelf serves no purpose either.") establish Gabriel's dry wit and Clara's precision simultaneously. The banter never feels forced or anachronistic—it reads as genuinely Victorian in register while remaining accessible. Clara Vale is an exceptionally well-drawn protagonist. Her pride, her financial anxiety, her grief for her father, and her romantic feelings are all rendered through action and implication rather than statement. The detail of her turning past the page about tweezers quickly is devastating in its restraint. Her anger at Gabriel's offer of private money is psychologically precise—she understands exactly what it would mean for her reputation and independence, and the accusation she makes ("an inexpensive conscience and a woman willing to keep using the window") is both unfair and comprehensible, which is exactly right. Gabriel is somewhat less fully realized but still nuanced. His admission of shame—"I was ashamed of my own judgment being questioned"—is the kind of honest self-knowledge that elevates him above the typical romantic hero. His architectural profession is integrated naturally rather than decoratively. The pacing is excellent. Each chapter advances both the plot and the relationship in measured increments. The story earns its romantic resolution through accumulated small moments: the ladder carried to the gate, the biscuit left on the floor, the fire's damper, the bracket removed from the stairs. These details accumulate into genuine intimacy. The world-building is light but effective. The manor's social hierarchy (Pritchard, Mrs. Finch, the kitchen maid), the financial precarity of a Victorian tradesperson, the gendered obstacles Clara faces—all are present without being lectured about. **Weaknesses and criticisms:** The Pritchard subplot, while functional, is somewhat schematic. He serves primarily as an obstacle and is resolved rather too neatly in Chapter 7. His revelation that the cousin's extravagance was the real problem adds some complexity, but his character never quite transcends the role of antagonist-who-turns-out-to-have-had-reasons. The proposal scene in Chapter 8 is charming but slightly too neat in its resolution of the practical difficulties. Clara raises real objections about the shop's location, and Gabriel's "I had got as far as hoping you would say yes" is endearing, but the practical questions are essentially deferred rather than resolved. This is a minor complaint—the story is wise enough not to pretend they're solved—but it does leave the ending feeling slightly incomplete. Occasionally the prose reaches for a slightly too-polished aphorism: "Ten pounds looked substantial in a gentleman's study. Divided between an invoice, the rent and three weeks of household expenses, it became a collection of inadequate little sums." This is good writing, but it's the kind of sentence that knows it's good writing. There are a handful of such moments, though they never tip into purple prose. The Mrs. Finch scene in Chapter 6 is one of the story's best—the exchange about the shawl and the wages is perfectly calibrated—but her role as a kind of moral chorus is occasionally a little too convenient. The prompt ("One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows") is used as an opening line and then developed as a recurring motif throughout, culminating in the final joke about lending Gabriel a ladder. This is faithful, creative, and well-integrated. Overall, this is sophisticated, controlled, emotionally intelligent fiction. Its restraint is its greatest virtue—it trusts the reader and trusts its characters. The transformations feel earned because they are built from accumulated specific detail rather than declared. Initial Writing Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write a short story set in Wales. Task: write a short story over several chapters. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The story takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the first scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. The story will progress beyond this synopsis, and it's up to you where it goes.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write a short story set in Wales. Task: write a short story over several chapters. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The story takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the first scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor&#x27;s charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas.
